senses: A pair of eyebrows which meet in the middle.
examples: Actually - the unibrow look was never in.

senses: Having a distinct preference for intervals of fourths.
A manned vehicle that flies through the sky.
ety: From sky + ship; compare spaceship, landship.

senses: An annoyance or grievance.
The art or sport of horseriding; the skill required for it.
The money given to hunters, at the death of a fox, in order to buy ale.
ety: From Middle English arvell, from Old Norse erfiǫl (“a funeral feast”), from arfr (“inheritance”) + öl (“ale”). Cognate with Danish arveøl (“a wake, funeral feast”). More at erf, ale.

senses: Having a waffle-like pattern of intersecting creases.
examples: The US "pineapple" grenade's iron outer surface was waffled to aid its fragmentation into jagged shrapnel when it exploded.
Nate and Amy were waiting in the lobby of the Maui county jail in Wailuku, sitting in metal chairs designed to promote discomfort and waffled butt skin.
You have seen catering trucks: shiny stainless steel that is waffled with creases that look like diamonds.

senses: The process of assimilation, by a society, of the customs and practices of western culture.
examples: According to anthropology professor Peter Rigby, the Maasai's resistance to Westernization and their reluctance to enter the market system is ethnosuicide.

senses: The removal of mystery or confusion surrounding a topic or idea.
A rebate on the rake paid by a poker player.
In some arthropods, the second segment of the leg, between the coxa and the femur.
ety: From French trochanter, from Ancient Greek τροχαντήρ (trokhantḗr).

senses: A toy weapon consisting of a tube through which dried peas or small objects are blown.
A person who uses such a device.
An Indian sweet consisting of a flour-based outer skin filled with coconut and jaggery.
ety: Borrowed from Hindi and Marathi मोदक (modak).
examples: She serves the prasad, small cone-shaped bright-yellow modaks that they eat whole after touching to their foreheads to absorb god's blessing.

senses: One of the five canons of classical rhetoric: the method used for the discovery of arguments.
ety: From Latin inventiō. Doublet of invention.

senses: A small piece of aluminum foil or parchment paper, wrapped around food during cooking.
A small piece of paper used to roll up hair to make it curl.
examples: Remove from the oven and allow to rest for about 5 minutes before opening the papillote. Be very careful when you open it, since the papillote fills up with steam while it's cooking and it can be very hot.

senses: Fabrication, such as building or sculpting, at the nanoscale, on the level of individual molecules.
A spiral-shaped shell, especially that of a snail.
ety: Borrowed from Latin cochlea (“a snail”), from Ancient Greek κόχλιας (kókhlias, “a snail with a spiral shell”).

senses: Synonym of real school.
ety: From German Realschule, from real (“real”) + Schule (“school”), from the view that classical education at Gymnasia was not fit for the real world.

senses: One who earns money.
A profitable product or scheme; something that brings in good money.
examples: Those Japanese radios were a nice little earner: we sold all of them by lunchtime.
Substantial income from new video markets made Shaker Run New Zealand's top earner at Cannes, closely followed by The Quiet Earth.

senses: A traditional soft cake of Northern England, usually made with oatmeal and treacle.
ety: From Parkin, a diminutive of Peter.

senses: One who uses a sponge.
A parasitic hanger-on.
A person or vessel employed in gathering sponges from the sea.
A device for sponging cloth by means of a perforated adjustable cylinder.
Any naturally occurring magnet.
The focus of one's attraction or attention
ety: First attested from 1515, from Middle English lode (“guide”) + stone. From use as a guide tool by mariners. See also: lodestar.

senses: A telephone company (historically); a telecommunications company, a telecom.
ety: Diachronically, from tel + Co., from the collocation of Tel. Co. as seen, for example, in Bell Tel. Co. or the names of countless local telephone exchange companies (e.g., Savannah Valley Tel. Co., Mutual Tel. Co., Tarrytown Tel. Co.), by abbreviation in the late 19th through mid-20th centuries; synchronically also a clipped compound as tel(ephone) + co(mpany).

senses: To initialize again.
Of, being, or characteristic of a young, flirtatious girl.
examples: When Prince Andrew arrived at the house that evening, Maxwell was more coquettish than usual.

senses: A private viewing of an art exhibition before it opens to the public.
ety: From French vernissage, derived from the earlier habit of the artists to varnish their paintings the day before the opening of an exhibition.

senses: Synonym of piss clam.
ety: From Middle English pissere; equivalent to piss + -er (agent noun). The sense referring to a urinal formed from piss + -er (patient suffix).

senses: outlaw, bandit
ety: Borrowed from Swahili shifta, from Amharic ሽፍታ (šəfta).

senses: The sum of the various techniques used by modern nation-states to control not individual subjects but their entire populations, as contrasted with traditional modes of power based on the threat of death from a sovereign.
ety: From bio- + power, calque of French biopouvoir, coined by Michel Foucault.
examples: The third type of power, biopower, emerges from the eighteenth century onward, and is directed toward populations rather than individual bodies.

senses: In or pertaining to the common version or edition.
ety: From Latin vulgātus, past participle of vulgō (“publish, make common, cheapen”).

senses: The leading figures of the Daraawiish (i.e. commanders, governors, representatives, judges etc.) considered collectively.
The Daraawiish government.
Not in a holster.
examples: The sheriff kept his gun unholstered in case the cowboys started any trouble.

senses: Having the ability to combine; combinable, combinational or combining.
An obsolete name of the unit of length equal to one femtometre (10⁻¹⁵ m).
ety: Named after Italian physicist Enrico Fermi.

senses: A violent young gang member or a hooligan.
ety: From Russian друг (drug, “friend”), in which sense it is used in the invented slang Nadsat in Anthony Burgess's dystopian novel A Clockwork Orange (1962).

senses: Anything that clasps.
A Chinese green tea.
a book describing sufferings of martyrs
ety: From Middle English passional, from Late Latin passiōnālis; equivalent to passion + -al.

senses: Piper excelsum (syn. Macropiper excelsum), a shrub endemic to New Zealand.

ety: Borrowed from Arabic كَسْرَة (kasra, “a breaking”), instance noun of the verb كَسَرَ (kasara, “to break”).
